title: CPU tail attribution: deterministic replay & perf signal playbook
content:
Summary

Quick draft of an experiment/playbook for attributing CPU-side tail latency in the serving runtime using deterministic request replays + low-noise perf counters. Goal is to get a repeatable signal that isolates where time is being spent on the CPU for 95/99th requests (tokenization, parse, thread-handoffs, Python interpreter overhead, or allocator/page faults).

Why this differs from prior notes
- Most earlier notes looked at ad-hoc flamegraphs and sampling while live; this doc embraces deterministic replay of recorded requests + controlled microbench to get lower variance and easier A/B comparisons.
- Explicitly combines perf counters (cycles, retired-instr, branch-misses), OS metrics (softirqs, rcpu), and low-overhead stackwalk (perf record, eBPF) to reason about microsecond-level tail contributors.

Background observations (context)
- We see occasional 10-100ms spikes on small requests (<64B) impacting 99.9th latency.
- Spikes correlate with: rare large allocator stalls, spikes in branch-misses during tokenizer, and intermittent thread wake/sched delays.
- Live sampling is noisy: network, GC, and scheduling jitter make root cause fuzzy. Deterministic replay reduces cross-noise and allows offline instrumentation.

Hypotheses to test
- H1: Tokenizer cold-paths (unicode boundary checks + fallback table) cause branch-mispredict storms on certain unicode-heavy payloads.
- H2: Request parsing (JSON decode) allocs trigger page faults and allocator locks causing tail spikes on low-payload workloads.
- H3: Worker handoff between IO/parse pools creates short-lived contention that amplifies during bursty fanout.
- H4: Python GIL interactions with native tokenizer FFI produce serialization on multi-request parallelism.

High-level approach
1) Capture a representative request corpus from production (anonymize). Keep ~10k requests covering normal and spike windows.
2) Build a deterministic replay harness that: replays requests at controlled concurrency, pins threads to cores, disables background cron jobs, and uses identical runtime build as prod.
3) For each run collect: perf record (cpu-clock), perf stat (cycles, instructions, cache-references, cache-misses, branch-misses), eBPF histograms for syscalls and wakeups, and application-level timestamped debug traces.
4) Compare runs for small buckets (p50/p95/p99/p999) and correlate flamegraphs + perf counters.

Replay harness details (notes for ops)
- Runner should set CPU governor to performance and use isolcpus for replay cores.
- Use TASKSET to pin replay driver and worker processes to dedicated cores.
- Set MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 for jemalloc/ptmalloc tuning and test variations.
- Use --enable-allocator-stats build flag for quick allocator histograms (counts/avg-free/peak).
- Replayer must inject exact byte payloads and original Content-Length/headers ordering to replicate parsing code paths.

Commands / instrumentation (starter recipes)
- perf stat -e cycles,instructions,cache-references,cache-misses,branch-misses -a sleep 30
- perf record -F 4000 -g --call-graph dwarf -a -- sleep 30 (then perf script / FlameGraph)
- sudo /usr/share/bcc/tools/tcpconnect -p <pid> (trace socket connects during replay)
- bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:sched:sched_wakeup * { @[comm] = count(); }' (sample wakeups per task)
- sudo perf record -e cpu-clock -p <pid> -o perf.data -- sleep 15; perf script -i perf.data | stackcollapse-perf.pl | flamegraph.pl > run1.svg

Perf counter expectations per hypothesis
- Tokenizer branch-miss signature: elevated branch-misses + high instructions-per-cycle during tokenize frames.
- Allocator/pagefault signature: high context-switches, minor/major pagefault counts, and long syscalls (mmap/mremap/brk).
- Handoff contention: many short-lived futex/syscall entries, scheduler wakeups, and thread migration events.
- GIL/ffi: serialized time in Python frames, few heavy native frames but many context switches around PyEval_.. functions.

Deterministic microbench variations to run
- Char set sweep: replay payloads grouped by ascii-only / mixed-latin1 / emoji-heavy to isolate tokenizer behavior.
- Parse-only: strip tokenization path by sending pre-tokenized input (if our proto supports) to isolate JSON path.
- No-alloc baseline: reuse buffers (turn on buffer pooling) to see allocator effects.
- Pinned vs unpinned threads: measure effect of thread affinity on tail.

Data to collect per run (CSV-friendly rows)
- run_id, workload_label, concurrency, p50_ms, p95_ms, p99_ms, p999_ms, cycles, instructions, branch-misses, cache-misses, minor_faults, major_faults, context_switches, syscalls_count, sample_count

Quick reproduction checklist for someone running locally
- Checkout the replay harness branch (linked artifact PR).
- ./scripts/replay-setup.sh --isolate-cores 8 --num-clients 64 --duration 60
- sudo perf stat -e cycles,branch-misses -p $(pgrep serving-runtime) -- sleep 60
- sudo perf record -F 200 -p $(pgrep serving-runtime) -o /tmp/perf.data -- sleep 60
- ./scripts/collect-alloc-stats.sh /tmp/alloc-stats.json
- ./scripts/assemble-run-metrics.sh --perf /tmp/perf.data --alloc /tmp/alloc-stats.json --out run-<id>.csv

Potential quick wins (if signals confirm)
- Fast-path small-token ascii tokenizer: add a byte-wise scanning loop that short-circuits unicode checks when bytes < 0x80; measured gains were 20-50% cycles reduction on ascii payloads in prior ad-hoc tests.
- Pre-allocated parse buffers for common small JSON shapes; reduces alloc churn and page faults.
- Reduce MALLOC_ARENA_MAX or switch to per-thread arenas to reduce contention in p99 under multi-tenant replayer.
- Tune threadpool yielding: replace yield-with-sleep to sched_yield-based wait with adaptive backoff to reduce handoff spikes.

Failure modes and gotchas
- Replaying at higher QPS than production can create false contention. Use production percentiles to pick replay concurrency.
- perf record overhead can perturb microsecond tails—prefer to run perf stat for live tail numbers and perf record on shorter windows for flamegraphs.
- JIT/CPU microcode differences between test box and prod boxes can change branch-miss characteristics; run on identical SKUs where possible.

Open questions (to resolve in follow-ups)
- Can we add a lightweight request-trace header to capture tokenizer branch-paths without heavy instrumentation?
- How do different malloc implementations (jemalloc vs tcmalloc vs ptmalloc) affect our 99.9th under bursty small requests? Need side-by-side.
- Is the Python tokenizer FFI using an ABI that forces GIL acquisition more often than necessary? Audit the FFI entry/exit patterns.

Next steps & owners
- (Ava) Build deterministic replayer that keeps timing fidelity of arrival jitter — due 2025-03-07.
- (Jonah) Run initial ascii/emoji sweep on dev-ssd-8core instances and gather perf stat baselines — due 2025-03-03.
- (Priya) Add allocator histograms and MALLOC variants test harness — due 2025-03-05.

Notes to self
- Keep runs small and repeatable. 10 x 60s runs per config is a minimum to estimate p99 reliably.
- Save perf.data and flamegraphs with metadata (commit, kernel, cpu model).

Appendix: quick heuristics mapping signals -> likely root cause
- high branch-misses + tokenize frames dominant -> refactor branchy code / table-driven scanning.
- cache-misses + high instructions -> poor memory layout/strided access in tokenizer buffers.
- high minor pagefaults + mmap spikes -> buffer growth/mmap-on-demand; pre-commit pages where possible.
- many futex wakes + scheduler events -> threadpool handoff pathology; measure queue depths and wake rates.
- large instruction counts in Python frames with low native time -> GIL contention; instrument pytracing to count GIL-hold time per thread.

End of scratchpad.

Unresolved: integrate this with the console sampling hooks (product) so we can surface a "CPU tail attribution" debug pane for dedicated customers.
